henry-davis-cuthbert-1885-08-09.A1:
Another Brutal Outrage.
CUTHBERT, Ga., Aug. 9.—Henry Davis, a negro, made a brutal assault on Sylva Knight, agen 9, daughter of the Baptist minister of this place, as she was walking through the woods. The child was horribly injured. The negro was captured and a mob attempted to lynch him, but the father of injured girl begged them to let the law take its course, so they finally acceded to his requests. The child's condition is critical.
henry-davis-cuthbert-1885-08-09.A3:
HANGED AND THEN SHOT.
LYNCHING FOLLOWS AN OUT-
RAGE IN RANDOLPH.
The 9-Year-Old Daughter of a Baptist Minister the Victim of a Naked Negro's Lust—The Little One Seized in the Road While Going to School.

CUTHBERT, GA., Aug. 9.—A hundred men, disguised by masks and armed with guns and revolvers, appeared in front of the jail at this place at 2 o'clock this morning and demanded the surrender of Henry Davis, a negro, aged 19 years, charged with despoiling a pretty little white child but 9 years of age. The jailer refused to accede to the demands of the crowd, and warned them not to advance on peril of their lives.

ATTACKING THE JAIL.

A shout of defiance was the only heed paid the admonition, and a moment later improvised battering-rams in sturdy hands were forcing open the portals of the jail. The jailer was absolutely at the mercy of the attacking party and the corridor to the cells was soon swarming with the masked avengers.

LED TO THE SLAUGHTER.

The iron bars to the cell in which Davis was confined were not sufficient to protect him, and 15 minutes after the first attack he was being dragged between armed men to the railroad bridge. Arriving at their destination, the captors encircled the neck of their victim with a slip-noose and throwing the other end of the rope over a sill of the bridge gave a pull altogether, and swung Davis' struggling body between heaven and earth. Strangulation would soon have completed its work, but before it had time to do so a volley of bullets, which completely perforated Davis' body, ended his misery.

THE CRIME.

The crime for which Davis was so tragically executed was one of the most revolting ever perpetrated in this county. Sylvia Knight, aged 9 years, and her brother, aged 7, children of Rev. John T. Knight, of Ward's Station, left their home Friday morning to go to school. They carried their books and dinner basket and were wished a God speed as they trudged along the road by the kind-hearted mother who stood on her piazza watching them recede from view.

A HORRIBLE APPARITION.

The little ones had reached a spot three-fourths of a mile from home when a naked negro sprang out into the roadway before them and seized the little girl in his arms. The children screamed with terror. The negro ran into the woods with the little one in his arms, leaving her terrorized brother crying in the highway, and threatened with death if he made a move or further outcry. Having accomplished his horrible purpose the negro fled into the woods, releasing the little girl. Bruised and bleeding she ran home with her brother, and told the story of the outrage to herald parents. Both children testified that they could identify the nude assailant, and each said that he had a large scar on one of his hips.

PURSUIT AND CAPTURE.

Rev. Mr. Knight and an armed posse of neighbors scoured the woods, and made prisoners of five or six negroes on suspicion. The captives were taken before the children, and Davis was identified at sight. An examination of his person revealed the scar on the hip which the children had described. Lynching would have followed immediately had it not been for Rev. Mr. Knight's request that the law be allowed to take its course. Public indignation continued to increase, however, and its culmination was the tragedy of this morning.
henry-davis-cuthbert-1885-08-09.A5:
THE PEOPLE SETTLED WITH HIM.
A Negro who had Abused a Little Girl Hanged and Riddled with Bullets.

CUTHBERT, Ga., Aug. 9.—At 4 o'clock this morning 100 masked men appeared before the jail at this place and demanded that the jailer surrender Henry Davis, a negro aged 19 years, charged with assaulting a little girl. The jailer refused to comply with their demand. The crowd then battered its way into the jail and found Davis in his cell. He made an effort to resist, but several revolvers pointed at his head quieted him. He was then led to a railroad bridge near by, hanged to a rafter, and riddled with bullets before strangulation had ended his life.

On Friday Sylvia Knight, aged 9 years, and her brother, aged 7, left home with their lunch basket and books to attend school. Their father is the Rev. John T. Knight of the Baptist church here, and lives two miles from town. Three-quarters of a mile from home a nude negro leaped from the bushes by the roadside, and confronted the children. He seized the girl and carried her into the woods, leaving her brother standing in the road paralyzed with fear. After a while the negro fled. The children, both nearly crazy with terror, and the little girl, covered with blood and bruises, ran home and related their experience to their parents. They said the negro had a scar on his right hip. Armed men were soon scouring the woods, and eventually captured Davis. The children identified him at sight, and an examination of his body revealed the scar reported by the little ones. A hundred men surrounded the captive and threatened to tear him limb from limb. The pastor and father begged that the law be allowed to take its course, and through his entreaties Davis was taken to jail.

Last night, however, the indignation of the community had reached such a pitch that its culmination in this morning's tragedy could not be prevented.

henry-davis-cuthbert-1885-08-09.A16:
A DEMON'S DEED.
A Negro's Horrible Crime Near Ward s.
the community around Ward's Station was shocked last Friday over a fiendish outrage committed by Henry Davis on the person of a little white girl.

Little Sylvia Knight, aged nine years, and her smaller brother, aged seven years, the children of the Rev. John T. Knight, a Baptist minister and a farmer of high standing, left their home for school, a walk which carried them two miles south of Ward's station. Their mother had prepared their buckets for them and after kissing them good-bye, watched them as they walked hand in hand down the country road until they were out of sight.

After the children had progressed on their journey about three-quarters of a mile they

WERE SUDDENLY POUNCED UPON by a burly negro, perfectly nude, who had been lying in wait behind a large stump by the road side. Seizing the little girl in his powerful grasp and commanding the little boy in thundering tones to remain in the road or die, he carried the victim, torn, choked, bleeding and frightened almost to death, to a place of concealment where he treated her in a horrible and most outrageous manner and escaped into the woods adjoining.

Crazed with fear almost to the verge of insanity the children returned home as rapidly as possible and told their terrible story to father and mother. In a partial description gotten from them it was stated among other things
LARGE SCAR ON HIS HIP.

Public indignation was at fever heat and a posse of men armed with shot-guns, rifles, pistols, knives, clubs, etc., went in his pursuit. When some half dozen or more had been arrested they were taken in a body to the house of the grief stricken parents. As they approached the dwelling the little girl recognized the demon who assaulted her, and turning to her mother, exclaimed:

"Mother, there is the very one, and if they will search him they will see the scar."

The scoundrel proved to be Henry Davis, a desperately mean negro, about nineteen years old, and in the employ of Colonel H. Crittenden, of Ward's station. He was carried before Dr. Bridgeman and proved to be the scoundrel wanted, not only by the scar upon his person, but by statements and proof uncontradicted.

The negro was taken to Cuthbert and lodged in jail and Saturday night about sixty or seventy-five citizens broke him out, hung him and perforated his body with bullets. This human fiend met a quick and deserved fate.
henry-davis-cuthbert-1885-08-09.A19:
ITEMS IN THREE STATES.
GEORGIA, FLORIDA AND SOUTH
CAROLINA PUT IN TYPE.
Serious Results of a Runaway at Marietta—A Hunt After Wild Hogs at Montezuma—The Birth and Growth of the Prohibition Movement in Georgia.

GEORGIA.

Rockdale Superior Court convened yesterday.

J. P. Miller, formerly of Talbotton, is now proprietor of the Altoona house, at Altoona, Fla.

Jesse Allen, of Athens, has a large white rat in his store that kills every gray rat he comes across.

A surgical operation, performed by an Atlanta physician, resulted in the death of W. P. Young, of Marietta.

A. R. Wilson, of Morgan county, has two moocasin snakes, each having double heads, in two bottles of alcohol.

The City Council of Albany has voted in favor of extending the city limits so as to include the fair grounds and the new cemetery.

Rev. James A. Clement, of Rome, has completed a work of several hundred pages, entitled "History of Rome and Cherokee, Ga."

Frank Nash, pitcher for the Columbus club, who had been sick with typhoid fever, died Sunday morning. He was buried Sunday afternoon.

Mrs. William Betsel, of Marietta, suffered a broken arm by being thrown from her buggy. Saturday. Her husband and child were painfully bruised.

"Dummy," a deaf and dumb negro prisoner made a truittess effort to deal station house keeper George L. Henry a deadly blow with a plank Saturday morning.

At Buchanan, Hon. Charles Taliaferro got struck on the back of his neck with a piece of timber while at work at his saw mill, a few days ago. He was not able to be taken to his home.

A drummer was in Lumpkin last week who carried a piece of the rope with which a negro was lynched in Cuthbert in his vest pocket. He says it beats a rabbit foot for luck.

At Alapaha, Friday, one of Silas O'Quin's sons had two of his fingers torn off while trying to hold a horse that had been frightened by a clap of thunder. The wound is a very severe one.

Capt. Price Perkins, Dr. J. A. Thornton, and Clifford Harrison, of Lumpkin, went out about Richland for a day's sport among the doves, and succeeded in killing 13, Dr. Thornton bagged 78.

At Cartersville, Friday, Col. R. H. Jones, the President of the Jones Sons Manufacturing Company, had the middle finger of his right hand cut off by a rip saw. His hand was otherwise torn by the saw.

At practice at American Saturday afternoon, Messrs. Hitt, Chapman, Myrick and Ross put sixty shots into four targets, that, with the exception of one shot, never varied over an inch from the bull's-eye, at a distance of twenty yards.

Deputy Sheriff Holder, of Lumpkin, went to Eufaula Saturday after a negro man named Charley Chin, who is in jail there awaiting removal to Stewart county to answer an indictment found against him 4 years ago for beating to death a horse belonging to A. D. Chambliss.

Lightning struck a large oak tree standing in front of A. D. Chambliss' house, four miles north of Lumpkin. The tree was of giant growth, and was literally shattered, a large piece of the tree being thrown over the house. Two of Mr. Chambliss' daughters were severely shocked and it was probably an hour and a half before one of them was fully restored.

Notice is given that application will be made to the General Assembly at its present session for the passage of an act authorizing the Mayor and Council of Athens to submit to the qualified voters of said city the question of altering the contract made with the Richmond and West Point Terminal Company in reference to the sale and extension of the Northeastern railroad and for other purposes.

Friday night bold work was done by some thief or thieves at Rome. At Peacock's saloon an entrance was effected by chiseling through a 14-inch wall. The saloon had closed at 11:80 that night, and when it was opened Saturday morning a hole 12 by 18 inches was found in the back wall. Only a box of cigars and two bottles of whisky had been stolen. Money was evidently the object of the thieves, but Mr. Peacock had left none in the cash drawer.

Just above the lower ferry, near Montezuma, there is quite a large island inhabited by wild boots. They swim the river, and then proceed to destroy Mr. Fletch Norris' corn. Tuesday he organized a crowd of men, armed with shotguns, and proceeded to the spot where they were in the habit of taking their meals. In a short time five of them had been killed, some of them weighing from 150 to 155 pounds. The hogs have been on the river since last September, whether they went in search of beach mast. Over 50 bushels of corn has been destroyed by them within the past week.

Georgia started out as a prohibition colony. The trustees issued an order at the beginning that the selling and drinking of rum in Georgia should be absolutely prohibited. Wine-making, however, was encouraged, and in a short time the colonists began to fall into habits of drunkenness. In 1744 stringent laws were passed against intemperance, but it was too late. The liquor men got the upper hand and kept it for a long time. The next great temperance movement in Georgia began about 1845 and lasted ten years. Father Mathew's work bore good fruit, and temperance lectures were almost as common throughout the State as they are now. Unfortunately the question got into politics, and in 1855 the Hon. B. H. Overby ran for Governor on a prohibition ticket. He was defeated by a large majority and reform waned and died out until the beginning of the present agitation about fifteen years ago.

FLORIDA.

Lake City wants an ice factory and a dairy farm.

There were but five deaths in Jacksonville last week.

A hotel, costing $10,000, is nearing completion at Seville.

The Fort Meade district of Polk county has 1,460 inhabitants.
henry-davis-cuthbert-1885-08-09.A20:
ITEMS FROM THE SOUTH.
At Plattaburg, Mo., the Central Hotel and two stores adjoining were destroyed by fire, causing a loss of $25,000.

HARRY DAVIS, who outraged Miss Minnie Gordon, at Cuthbort, Ga., was taken from jail by a mob of masked men and hanged to a bridge.

ANNA DAVENPORT, of Nashville, Tenn., compelled Millie Plummer's baby of 4 months to swallow concentrated lye, and poured the stuff over its body. The child when found was covered with blood and half of its leg eaten away. It will die. Anna, who was arrested, had fought with Millie and tortured her child in revenge. The women are colored.

The Attorney General has been urged to discontinue the criminal prosecutions instituted against the Oklahoma boomers, but has declined until he shall receive assurance that they have permanently and in good faith abandoned their attempts to the forbidden territory.

JOE POLLOCK, son of the proprietor of a flouring mill in Vincennes, Ind., who was stationed at Lone Oak, Tex., as railroad agent, has mysteriously disappeared. He has not been heard of or seen since the 4th of August, on which day he wrote a letter to his mother.

DAVID MARBLES, of Carrollton, Mo., who had been divorced from his wife two years, went to Coloma, where she lived, and shot her dead, after which he blew his own brains out.

The daughter of a planter named Vanderwer, living fifteen miles west of Dallas, Texas, was burned to death by the explosion of kerosene which she used to start a fire. Her brother and sister were fatally burned.

While resisting arrest at Maysville, Ky., Jeff Phillips, colored, was shot and killed by Deputy Marshal Baugher.

HENRY FRAKER, colored, was hanged at Catlettsburg, Ky., for the murder of Chester Hounker last May. The execution was public, and was witnessed by three thousand persons.

WATT M. GRAY, of North Middletown, Ky., purchased $20,000 worth of cattle from Bourbon County farmers, took them to New York and sold them for $18,000 and disappeared. Parties brought attachments for alleged worthless checks, but his farm was mortgaged for its full value—$20,000.

THE Southern Exposition at Louisville, Ky., opened with elaborate ceremonies. Excursion trains were run from all directions and the buildings are crowded.

The Secretary of War has instructed Gen. Miles, of the Department of the Missouri, to hold troops in readiness to enforce the President's recent proclamation in relation to cattlemen on the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservations. By the terms of the proclamation cattlemen will be compelled to remove herds by Sept. 4.* The troops will be held at Fort Reno.

BENNETT B. SIMMONS, of New Orleans, has been appointed chief of the Special Agents' Division of the General Land Office, vice Alfred G. McKenzie, who has been appointed special agent.

The Secretary of the Interior has authorized the Indian office to pay out $68,000, the proceeds of the sale of certain lands in Kansas for the redemption of Kaw Indian script. The amount of the script outstanding is $120,000, of which $85,000 has been presented. The available funds will not be quite sufficient to pay the principal and interest of the script presented, and they will be divided pro rata among the script holders.

keyport-keyport-1885-08.A1:
Ocean Grove.
Saturday was "Women's Foreign Missionary Day," and large enthusiastic meetings were held. The thirteenth annual reports were read at the afternoon session. The services were continued and concluded Sunday. In the morning Rev. Dr. J. P. Newman preached in the large auditorium before an audience of at least 6000 people. He had occupied the same pulpit a year before, when General Grant was present and received and ovation from the multitude.

Several times during the discourse the speaker was applauded. When he had finished a large collection was taken up for the purpose of the Missionary Society.

The Camp Meeting exercises will begin at Ocean Grove Wednesday morning, when Bishop Andrews will preach the opening sermon. The meeting will continue until the 28th.

Shrewsbury.

On Thursday evening, July 30th, Library Hall, Shrewsbury, was filled with an attentive audience, in response to an announcement that an entertainment would be given in aid of the Altar Guild of Christ Church, Shrewsbury. The programme was as follows:—Selections by Mr. F. H. Paulison; the play, "Change of Base," Dramatis personnae: Capt. Dashwood, G. D. Tallman; Mr. Tarbox, H. Campbell; Miss Prim, Mrs. A. N. Jennings; Flora Fayaway, Miss H. Franklin. One of Alstrom's pianos was used. The most pleasing feature of the entertainment was the singing by Master Willie Howland, accompanied by Miss Franklin.

An invitation by Mr. Paulison was given for all present to remain for dancing. The above gentleman gave ganeedotes and songs and performed well on the harmonicum. All who have seen and heard this band of ameteur actors and actresses may imagine the success of their efforts.

While paying toll, on Friday last, at Wolf Hill, Mr. John Trafford, of Shrewsbury, with a lady friend, were in danger of a smash up as a gentleman from Long Branch ran into their buggy and nearly demolished one of the hind wheels. The lady was taken home by Mrs. VanVleit somewhat frightened. The drive towards Long Branch is a precarious one.

On Monday, August 17, Mable, daughter of John and Linie Eyeles, died of dysentary after a painful illness of a week, aged 4 years. One of the most interesting children in the village, the sympathy of the community is given the parents.

A Shrewsbury couple were nearly overturned in the vicinity of Turtle Mill, and the subsequent results of that drive were vastly important to this couple at least. Let all that read this take notice.

While the Street Commissioner with his men were cutting down a tree on Pine street, Keyport, on Tuesday morning of last week, it fell upon the butcher wagon of Mat. Pease, throwing some of the meat out and smashing things generally. Mrs. James Flett, who was standing near the wagon, saw the meat under the fallen tree and thinking it was one of the children, fainted away, and it was a number of hours before she regained consciousness.

The propeller Wyckoff, says the Matawan Journal, being unable to carry the enormous freights being shipped by our farmers, the company had for a time hired the oyster sloop Frazer, of Keyport, owned by Charles Britton. On Thursday night she left Matawan at about 9.30, ladened with 300 crates of tomatoes and a small quantity of other stuff. About half-way between the propeller wharf and the brick-yards, in making one of the short turns in our crooked creek she ran heavily ashore and could not be gotten off as the tide was ebbing. As the tide fell it left her stern so low that she would not come up with the rise and the salt water ran into the hold and damaged the freights, causing a loss of about $100. The sloop was lightened and gotten off the next day, without damage to the vessel.

Last week's Keyport Enterprise says: For several Saturday nights of late this town has been visited by men from the Big Woods, who make the night hideous with their goings on, fighting, cursing, tearing fences down and in other ways disturbing the peace and destroying property. Last Saturday night was the climax. Several of this gang attacked a man in front of the hotel and he retreated to the store next door, being followed by the Big Wood's rowdies. This store is kept by colored people and they at once ordered the gang out. One of the Big Woodsers took a chair and made an assault on the proprietor, and the latter in turn threw a bottle which struck one of the gang on the forehead making a terrible gash. After the Big Woodsers got outside they made a rush and broke in the entire store front. Brickbats flew thick and fast and there was a regular melee. It is hoped that the authorities will prosecute the offenders to the end and several warrants have been issued. Unless this is done a movement will be made to organize a band who will meet these loafers on their next visit to town and proceed to clean them out, in a manner similar to that in which they were driven from Keyport years ago. Something must be done and that soon. During the above racket three shots were fired by the darkies, but none took effect.

At, Their Old Tricks. Chattanooga, Aug. 20—A special to the Post Dispatch says there is intense excitement in Dalton, Ga., this morning over a visit paid that place by a band of kukl ux last night. Fifty men, well disguised, entered the city shortly after midnight. They visited a house of ill-fame owned by Mrs. Jane Kidd. Six of her boarders were dragged from their beds and each given fifty lashes. Some of the women are in a critical condition and may die. The band then went to the house of Tom Carver, a noted thief, and beat him to death—after torturing him for half an hour. Another negro named Armstead is so terribly beaten that he will die. The mob then notified several persons to leave town at once or they would be killed. No clew can be found to the identity of any of the band. A Disgusted Greenbacker.
A Disgusted Greenbacker.

Cedar Rapids, Aug 20—Elias Doty, who worked the greenback vote of this county up to over five hundred, publishes a card in, the Gazette this evening to the greenbackers of Iowa, announcing himself for governor. He says: "Whereas, our party leaders have for the second time presumed to trade our votes to the democratic party; and whereas, there is a time when forbearance ceases to be a virtue. I therefore announce to the true greenbackers of Iowa that I am a bona fide greenbacker and a candidate for the office of governor. and respectfully ask the support of all greenbackers whose manhood and self-respect will not allow them to be sold like slaves by their master—the devil.

The Impending Strike.

St. Louis Aug. 20—There are no

St. Louis, Aug. 20—There are no new developments in the impending strike of the Knights of Labor to-day. A. C. Coughlin of the Wabash committee said this morning that the committee does not anticipate any trouble for three or four days, and very likely for a week. The southwestern system committee is authorized by the national executive committee to order a general strike in the west whenever it is deemed advisable, but a strike is not likely to be ordered within four days. There really have been no refusals to go to work as is now known.

Suspended.

Toledo Aug. 19—Welker & Co.

Suspended. Toledo, Aug. 19—Walker & Co., grain commission merchants, suspended today. The alleged cause is the refusal of the banks to accept their paper, but it is claimed that they are worth several times the amount of their indebtedness. They are winding up affairs and will go out of business at once. Liabilities small. The house is one of the oldest in the trade here.
tom-carver-dalton-1885-08-19.A2:
KU KLUX VISIT DALTON.
THE BAD ELEMENTS OF THE CITY ROUGHLY HANDLED.
Women of Ill-Fame Whipped and Their Houses Torn Down—The Negro Proprietor of One of the Dens Killed in the Melee—The Vigilants from Murray County.

DALTON, GA., Aug. 20.—Last night the ku klux or some other band of masked men, to the number of 50, entered Dalton and proceeded to administer justice to the evil-doers of the city. For some time past lawlessness and disorder have prevailed. Vagrants, tramps, thieves and lewd houses have accumulated, especially since the moral sensation has driven so many from Chattanooga. The masked regulators proceeded first to the house of Ormstead McKain (colored), who keeps a disreputable boarding house and where a number of black and white women were found, and here they severely whipped him, his wife and a colored boarder. McKain was so badly beaten that he was unable to get down to breakfast this morning.

TARVER KILLED.

The next place visited was that of Thomas Tarver, colored, who keeps a disreputable house near the Baptist College, on College hill. Tarver was taken out of his house to be whipped, but resisted, and in the melee was killed by a pistol shot, the ball taking effect in the back of his head. He was also crushed by a blow. The Coroner impaneled a jury this morning and held an inquest, the verdict being death from the causes above described, and at the hands of unknown parties. Tarver was a desperate character, a common thief, and a corruptor of the race to which he belonged.

A HOUSE SACKED.

The next place visited was that of Mrs. Kidd, a well-known white woman, who has kept a house of ill-fame near the cemetery for a number of years, and who has a son named Bill Kidd, a notorious thief. The mob sought to arrest and whip Bill, but he fired and ran, receiving in return about 20 shots after him as he ran away. The vigilants then tore up the house of Mrs. Kidd and gave her orders to leave the city.

ANOTHER HOUSE TORN DOWN.

The next place visited was Lizzie Wilson's (white), who lives in the southern portion of the city, and who, with a sister, keeps another disreputable establishment for the benefit of negroes (she has several negro children), and here the mob tore up the house and administered to Mrs. Wilson a severe whipping.

A WHITE MAN WARNED.

The regulators then went to Lizzie Lee's, a mulatto woman, on Hamilton street, where she keeps a disorderly boarding house, and left word for a certain white man who boards there to change his lodging or else the law would be administered. Other houses of a less notorious character were broken up and their occupants ordered to leave.

A CALL ON THE MAYOR.

The mob then went to the house of the Mayor, Col. Samuel P. Maddox, and called him out, commanding him and the City Council to administer the laws with a more salutary effect or else the city government would be taken into hand. They left with the Mayor a long list of idlers, loafers, suspected thieves and bad women whom, through the Mayor, they gave notice to leave the town or take the consequences in lieu of obedience to orders.

NOT A POLITICAL AFFAIR.

The affair has no political aspect or significance whatever. Not a good citizen, white or black, was molested, and the evil-doers, whether white or black, were severely dealt with without distinction. The people of Dalton deplore the necessity for such a step, although much sympathy is felt for the good effect produced. Some people, however, are quite indignant, and an indignation meeting may yet be called.

IN A STATE OF TERROR.

Dalton has been in a state of terror for a month on account of burglaries and tramps, several of whom have molested and attempted to outrage ladies and girls. A number of burglaries have been committed recently, and the city has been infested with loafers and vagrants.

THE MOB FROM MURRAY COUNTY.

No doubt this state of things has resulted in a secret call on the part of somebody for help from the kuklux. This band of mob lawyers is from Murray county, east of Dalton, and came into the
sutied in a secret call on the part of somebody for help from the kuklux. This band of mob lawyers is from Murray county, east of Dalton, and came into the city from that direction. Much excitement prevails and great regret is expressed at the death of Tarver, and that any excess should have occurred.
tom-carver-dalton-1885-08-19.A3:
Ku Klux in Georgia.
Another account.

Atlanta, Aug. 20. - Last night. night a band of ku klux, supposed to be from Murray county, went to Dalton and cleaned up the lawless element of that town. They went to a disreputable boarding house kept by Armstead Wickean and beat the occupants. Tom Turner's house, of a similar character, was visited. Turner offered resistance and was killed. Other houses were also visited and the occupants whipped. A white man, boarding with negroes, was ordered to leave town or suffer the consequences. The party visited the house of the widow Kidd, in search of Bill Kidd, a notorious man, and 25 or 30 shots were exchanged. It is not known whether Kidd was hurt or not. The Kidd establishment was demolished. It has long been disreputable. The mob took in all the disreputable houses, then went to the mayor's office and left a list of those under mob surveillance. The whole affair was an effort to rid Dalton of the bad characters that infest the town.
tom-carver-dalton-1885-08-19.A5:
KUKLUX IN GEORGIA.
KURLUX IN GEORGIA.
Outrages by a Masked Band of Men
Near Dalton.
[SPECIAL TO THE APPEAL.]
[SPECIAL TO THE APPEAL.]

CHATTANOOGA, TENN., August 20.—For several months past the citizens of Dalton, Ga., have been very much annoyed by the lawlessness of a disreputable set who lived about the suburbs, and recently they became very bold and peculiarly offensive. Last night a large body of armed men entered the town and proceeded to the various establishments. The inmates were in turn called to the door, then seized by the vigilantes and very severely flogged, and each one given notice in turn that unless they reformed the visit would be repeated. One man named Alfred Tarver resisted and was shot dead on the spot. Another named Armistead fled and was fired on four times and slightly wounded. Several women were flogged by the mob. They then visited the mayor and served notice on him that the laws against vagrancy must be more rigidly enforced and all lawless characters must be driven out. The proceeding has created the most intense excitement throughout North Georgia.
tom-carver-dalton-1885-08-19.A9:
Good Work by Ku Klux.
CHATTANOOGA, Tenn., Aug. 20. — There is intense excitement at Dalton, Ga., this morning over a visit paid that place by a band of Ku Klux last night. There were fifty men, well disguised, who entered the city shortly after midnight. They visited a house of ill fame owned by Mrs. Jane Kidd, and the woman and six girls were dragged from their beds and each one was given fifty lashes. Some of the women may die. The band then went to the house of Tom Carver, a noted thief, and beat him to death after torturing him for half an hour. Another negro, named Armsted, was so terribly beaten that he will die. The mob then notified several persons to leave the place at once, or they would be killed. No clue can be had as to the identity of any of the band.

The party visited the house of William Kidd in search of Bill Kidd, a notorious man, and twenty-five or thirty shots were exchanged. It is not known whether Kidd was hurt or not. The Kidd establishment was demolished, it being very disreputable. The mob took in all the disreputable houses, regardless of the color of the occupants, and then went to the mayor's office and left a list of those under mob surveillance. The whole affair was an effort to rid Dalton of the bad characters that infest the town.
tom-carver-dalton-1885-08-19.A16:
THE KILLING OF TARVER.
An Attack with an Ax on the Part of the
Nogro the Cause of His Death.
Danger Area. The Cause of his death.
An Attack with an Ax on the Part of the Negro the Cause of His Death.

DALTON. Aug. 21.—The facts in the killing of Thomas Carver by the Regulators in this city on Wednesday night last are about these: The Regulators were proceeding to whip a white woman close by, who was the mistress by the negro, and he attacked the party with an ax, very nearly killing one of them. He was commanded several times to put down the ax, but refused to do so, when he was shot by some one in the back, and as he ran off one of the party struck him a crushing blow in the back of the head. This is the report of an eye witness close by, and several witnesses heard the repeated command, "Put down the ax." "Put down the ax." Several parties heard a member of the band while riding through the streets say, "That — nigger like to got me," and another say, "I think I got him." Everything is now quiet in the city, the loafers, thieves, tramps and idlers have disappeared from the streets, the lewd houses are broken up and the bad women are leaving the city. The people of Dalton slept soundly last night for the first time in a month.
tom-carver-dalton-1885-08-19.A17:
LIFE AT DALTON.
Bad Characters no Longer Seen—Savannahians Summering in Whitfield.
DALTON GA. Aug 23. Since the visit
Bad Characters no Longer Seen—Savannahians Summering in Whitfield.

DALTON, GA., Aug. 23.—Since the visit of the Regulators, on Aug. 19, our streets have been free from loafers and idlers, and no more burglaries have been committed. Everything has settled down quietly, those who were notified to leave have done so, and no further trouble is anticipated.

The strange disease in the eastern part of the county, which was prevailing with fatal results, as reported by Dr. Bivings some weeks ago, is now reported to have entirely disappeared, and the health of the county is good. Our city is extremely healthy.

Dalton is fast making a reputation as a summer resort. Our hotels are crowded with visitors. Quite a number of Savannahians are spending the summer here. Mrs. Joseph F. Dasher and family, of Savannah, are with her brother, C. H. Snow, at Oak Grove, one mile from the city. Crops in the county are the best for years. Every indication points to the fact that Whitfield will not have her corn cribs and smoke houses in the West another year.—At the opera house last night the Dalton amateurs rendered the intensely interesting play "Above the Clouds" to a packed house. Messrs. Horne, Babcock, McKaney, Macauley, Loveman, Carpenter, and Holtzclaw were perfectly at home, and rendered their parts faultlessly. Mrs. Babcock, Misses Wotten, Cappes and Holtzclaw were perfection. Dalton is proud of her dramatic talent. The proceeds of the entertainment go to charitable purposes.

The following is the full text of the remarkable resolution posted in Dalton and sent to its Mayor by the band of Regulators which raided the town during the past week, killing Tom Tarver and seriously flogging and otherwise punishing several others:

"Notice to the Citizens of Dalton: Owl Hollow, Aug. 19, 1885.—Gentlemen: Our object is to protect the good people of Dalton, and especially the widows and orphans of the community, and what we do to-night will, in our judgment, afford them the best protection, and we hope the good people will approve. If there is any old fool who thinks different he had best keep his mouth closed, or we will serve him as the balance of thieves and robbers, and if there is anyone who attempts to encourage a sentiment in opposition to our project, we shall wipe him up.

“We are sore and tired of the congregation of bootblacks and loafers, white and black, who congregate around our public places, and if they do not quit it we will deal with them severely.

“They must go to work, and not be long about it, or we shall be back soon.

“We furthermore say that if any thief is caught breaking hous a or molesting friendless widows, they will be taken out and hung without ceremony. Further, we do not want any town dudes to interfere, as they have no discretion in this matter. We have taken it in hand and propose to run it. We earnestly request that if there is any more stea ing, or attempts, that notice be given our secretary, at Owl Hollow, and we will attend to it at once.

“We notify the following parties to leave Dalton at once:

“The Indian doctor, Wm. Jones, Tom Glenn, Tom Taryver and son John, Tom Baxter, Old Buster and family, all colored.

“Also Andrew Wrinkle must go, the women at the Palmer house and the women at the spring.

“Old Brother Prow must hunt him a white boarding house, or we shall be forced to deal with him according to our stringent laws.

“If old Mrs. Kidd keeps any more white boarders she will have to leave. William Kidd must leave Dalton.

“Armstead McCain must go to work, or he will have to get down and out. Mary McCain must not keep any more white boarders, or she will have to leave.

“Frank Keith, Alex Lovejoy and Will Broyles must go to work or leave.

“We mean business.

“Regular meetings at Owl Hollow Saturday nights. Call meetings when desired.

“On motion of the Willipus Willipus this body extend their thanks to Jack Broyles for the kind attention during the night, as pilot; and that these proceedings be placed on the minutes of the order. and a copy be furnished the Mayor and Council of Dalton. "We neglected to say that Jack Broyles had better take up his traps and leave immediately. REGULATORS." Early Schools of Sumter.
tom-carver-dalton-1885-08-19.A20:
DALTON'S MASKED REGULATORS.
Fifty masked men entered Dalton the other night and proceeded to take the management of the municipal affairs into their own hands. They whipped several negroes of disreputable character, gave notice to others to leave town, broke up houses of ill fame and finally shot and killed a negro man, who resisted with an axe their felonious depredations. A press dispatch says the mob came from Murray county. This is hardly probable, because it does not stand to reason. The citizens of Murray county are not likely to be so zealous in regulating the society of a town in another county, just for the fun of being classed in the category of outlaws themselves. It is too risky and dangerous, and besides these Daltonites did not encroach upon their interests. It is more than likely the maskers were residents not far from the corporate limits of Dalton. To say the least of it, it was a very unfortunate and disgraceful affair, and is a source of regret to all right thinking people.

While this mob was shooting, whipping and rioting in the town, where were the town officers that they did not summon a posse of citizens and protect the good order of their town by suppressing such unlawful proceedings? Certainly the outrages perpetrated are not to the credit of Dalton; for when a city becomes so badly infested with thieves, burglars, vagrants and "soiled doves" that the civil authorities are powerless as a corrective body, it reflects badly on the inefficiency of the town officers and the laxity of law. We trust Georgia will not have her reputation again blurred by mob rule. Heated passion and excited impulse are poor substitutes for doing equal justice to all men in the protection of life, liberty and property. When this mob started out to whip and frighten a few worthless characters, they had little idea that they would commit murder before their self-appointed mission ended, yet they dispersed to their homes with their hands dripping in the blood of a human being who had acted only on the defensive. The Governor should see to it that these maskers are ferreted out and punished. The severity with which they administered punishment, should by the law be administered to them. The only surprise is that the Governor has been so dilatory in the matter.

George Bermudez Against a
The Georgia Regulators Again at Work in the Neighborhood of Dalton.
[SPECIAL TO THE APPALACHIA]
CHATTANOOGA, TENN.
The Georgia
The Georgia Regulators Again at Work in the Neighborhood of Dalton.

CHATTANOOGA, August 31.—The Georgia regulators, whose recent visit to Dalton, Ga., caused such a tumult of excitement, are again on the warpath. On their last raid they whipped fifteen persons and killed a desperate negro who resisted. A few nights since they visited the house of a man named Perry, in Murray county, ten miles from Dalton. He was dragged from his bed at midnight and given a terrible whipping. It seems that Perry had been circulating slanderous reports regarding a well-known young lady, and was resorting to every measure to blacken her name. There were twenty men in the gang, all of whom were well disguised.
